title: Design the Duplicate-Detection Rule
skill: Designing a matching rule from failure cases
scenario: In earlier tiers the duplicate check just answered yes or no. Today you author the rule it runs. You have four real near-misses from the last quarter, and a naive 'same invoice number' check gets two of them wrong. Design the identity key, the lookback window, and what happens on an exact versus a partial match - then defend it.
input:
Cases the rule must handle correctly:
1. TRUE DUPLICATE: same vendor, same invoice number, same total as a paid invoice. Must be caught and rejected.
2. RESENT UNDER A NEW NUMBER: same vendor and same total as a paid invoice, but a new invoice number. A number-only check misses it.
3. SPLIT SHIPMENT: same vendor and same invoice number as a paid invoice, but a DIFFERENT total (a legitimate second delivery billed separately). A number-only check wrongly rejects it.
4. ALTERED TOTAL: same vendor and same invoice number as a paid invoice, but a higher total. Could be a correction - or fraud. Never auto-reject; a human must look.

Beacon's longest vendor billing cycle is about 60 days; some vendors reconcile quarterly. Governance: owner AP Manager, changes approved by the Controller. Version 1.0.0.
instructions: Set identityKey to the combination of fields that catches cases 1 and 2 without the false positives of a number-only check.
Set lookbackDays wide enough to cover the longest billing cycle (about 60-90 days).
Set exactMatchAction for a full identity-key hit (auto-reject as a duplicate).
Set partialMatchAction for a near hit like the split shipment or altered total (route to human review, never auto-reject).
Write a rationale that names the four cases, then record ruleName, version 1.0.0, owner, and approver and validate.
copilotPrompt: Design a duplicate-detection rule that catches a true duplicate and a resend-under-new-number without falsely rejecting a split shipment, and sends an altered-total case to a human. Return JSON with ruleName, version 1.0.0, owner AP Manager, approver Controller, identityKey (the field combination), lookbackDays as a number, exactMatchAction (auto-reject), partialMatchAction (human review), and a rationale naming the four cases.
successMessage: Duplicate rule designed. The identity key catches the real duplicates, the partial-match path protects the legitimate split, and the altered total goes to a human instead of a silent reject.

intro.heading: Before you design: a duplicate is whatever your key says it is

sections.title: The identity key IS the rule
sections.body: 'Duplicate' is not a fact in the world - it is whatever your identity key declares equal. A key of invoice-number-only calls the split shipment a duplicate and misses the resend. A key of vendor + number + total catches the resend's twin and lets the split through. Choosing the key is the whole design.

sections.title: Exact match and partial match are different actions
sections.body: A full key hit is a certain duplicate: auto-reject it, no human needed. A partial hit - same vendor and total but a new number, or same number but a new total - is ambiguous. It could be legitimate or it could be fraud, so it goes to a person. Auto-rejecting an ambiguous case hides fraud; auto-accepting it pays twice.

sections.title: The lookback window is a cost decision
sections.body: Compare against too short a history and a slow-reconciling vendor's duplicate slips through after the window closes. Compare against all history forever and the check gets expensive and flags ancient look-alikes. Size the window to the real billing cycles - here about 60 to 90 days.

sections.title: The rationale carries the cases
sections.body: The four cases are the test suite for your rule. A rationale that names them lets the next designer check your key against each one instead of rediscovering the failure modes the hard way. The validator checks shape and governance; the cases are yours to reason through.

takeaway.heading: You designed what 'duplicate' means
points: You chose an identity key, and that choice defined which invoices count as the same - the resend is caught and the split shipment is spared.
Exact and partial matches earned different actions: certain duplicates auto-reject, ambiguous ones go to a human, so neither double-payment nor fraud slips through silently.
The lookback window is a deliberate trade between coverage and cost, sized to real billing cycles rather than left at a default.
The four cases are the rule's test suite; a rationale that names them makes the next revision a review instead of an excavation.
The workflow can now decide what counts as a duplicate by a rule someone owns, versioned and defensible.
